source.title: Understanding the Dilemma of Unlearning for Large Language Models
source.authors: Qingjie Zhang; Haoting Qian; Zhi-Cong Huang; Cheng Hong; Min-Lie Huang; Ke Xu; Chao Zhang; Han Qiu

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether supposedly forgotten knowledge can be recovered through prompt-only keyword emphasis and argues that unlearning can disrupt access without erasing knowledge.
record.gate_note: The paper reports prompt-focus measurements in Table 1 and keyword-emphasis recovery rates in Table 2. It also describes a destructive-rate analysis in Figure 6, but the figure provides no numerical rates to extract. Hyperparameter selection results and cited recovery results from other papers are not results rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether 'forgotten' knowledge in post-unlearning models can be restored by changing only the prompt, without touching weights. It appends a keyword-emphasis phrase ('Focus On Key') and reports recovery rates for six unlearning methods on three datasets (Table 2). This is a new prompting-only method aimed at version E's question. The Table 1 focus-similarity analysis is a prompt-attribution stability measure, not a recovery rate or a deletion-versus-blocking test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that unlearning works by disrupting focus on answer-supporting prompt keywords rather than erasing knowledge. Emphasizing those keywords recovers much of it without weight changes. They attribute catastrophic forgetting to indiscriminate penalization of all prompt tokens. Existing methods are either recoverable or destructive, and reliable unlearning remains unachieved.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates six unlearning methods and introduces UNPACT and Focus On Key; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting attacks named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by dataset and unlearning method. The authors report smaller focus shifts on WMDP than News and distinct recovery rates across methods and datasets. Focus On Key also adds question tokens in some cases.

fits_no_version.finding: The proportion of cases keeping pre-unlearning KeyToken focus is lower for forgotten than retained items in every method-dataset cell. The drop averages 34.2pp on News, 21.4pp on Books and 6.3pp on WMDP (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearned items show reduced prompt-attribution overlap with the pre-unlearning model's key tokens (a black-box attribution signature of forgetting).

record.problems: Results are aggregated across the three models without model-specific values. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The study's destructive-rate analysis is shown in a plot without extractable numerical rates. Recovery depends on keywords identified using the pre-unlearning model and is incomplete and method-dependent.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's three across-method average retained and forgotten values (News 69.6%/35.4%, Books 49.6%/28.2%, WMDP 24.3%/18.0%) are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit while retaining the method-specific focus results and all reported Table 2 dataset-by-method recovery results.

untested.parts: Forget-set accuracy, chance levels and general-ability scores are not reported numerically. Hyperparameters were chosen for high forgetting and utility, but no numbers are given. The E results imply simple prompts do recover knowledge, including RMU on WMDP (R18).
No activation-direction ablation or internal analysis. The prompt-attribution focus analysis does not distinguish blocking from deletion.
Only keyword-emphasis suffixes were tested. Rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages and in-context information were not.
No robust counter-method is proposed or tested.

missing.what: Recovery rate and destructive rate across five training checkpoints per method, with epochs extended past the recommended values. Shown only as a plot with no numbers; it shows recoverability trading against collapse, e.g. NPOKL and RMU.
Per-model (Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B) recovery rates. Only aggregates across models are reported.

record.verdict_notes: The record's Table 1 Books TV/RMU values are misaligned: TV is 68.0/27.8 and RMU is 41.7/25.0. Recovery rates are relative to forgotten items (0% by construction under greedy decoding), so PROBAB is a second attack, not the baseline. The attack iterates over subsets of pre-unlearning key tokens and appends the question token. It therefore uses the pre-unlearning model and is effectively best-of-several prompts, which researchers should weigh when comparing with single-prompt attacks. The LLM judge is GPT-4o-mini. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report the targeted-knowledge accuracy and preserved general-ability results needed to test the full version, nor test whether simple attacks fail.
No fine-tuning or relearning-set recovery experiment.
Prompt attribution and keyword emphasis are studied; no activation-direction ablation or other internal activation edit is tested.
Tests explicit keyword emphasis in prompts only; does not test jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
No newer counter-method is tested for resistance to the attacks named in the claim.

tranche.reason: A new prompt-only attack (Focus On Key) aimed at the same recovery question. It does not reproduce the original methods. The reader's T5 is not needed.

source_check.notes: Table 2 gives Focus On Key against PROBAB (sampling, the paper's named baseline) by method and dataset, with no split over the 3 models, no n and no uncertainty. The no-attack recovery is 0 by definition. Focus On Key searches keyword subsets taken from the pre-unlearning model. The paper's own News NPOKL gain (30.5 vs 30.1) and News average (51.2 vs 50.25 cell mean) don't match its cells.

statements.correction: 2509.24675 introduces Focus On Key. It appends 'Focus on [keywords] to answer', with keywords taken from the pre-unlearning model's attributions, tries subsets of them, and decodes greedily. Table 2 is not split by model (Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B). NPOGD on News: 73.1% recovered (R3). GAGD on WMDP: 60.3% (R13). Six-method averages: News 51.2%, Books 30.7%, WMDP 54.4%.
statements.problem: Gives no result from this study. Its FocusOnKey numbers are credited to 2608.04519, and its conditions (TOFU, Harry Potter, Senators, multi-hop) leave out News and WMDP, where the cited rows R3 and R13 sit.

statements.correction: Focus On Key recovery for RMU: 9.5% on News (R6), 14.3% on Books (R12), 63.4% on WMDP (R18). Recovery rate counts forgotten items restored, so the no-attack level is 0.
statements.problem: Cites R6 and R12 under 'challenges', but this study's RMU recovery on News and Books is low, not absent. That is partial, so it belongs under limits_scope.

statements.correction: Same method across datasets: RMU 9.5% (News) / 14.3% (Books) / 63.4% (WMDP) (R6, R12, R18); GAGD 27.7 / 42.9 / 60.3 (R1, R7, R13). Six-method averages: News 51.2%, Books 30.7%, WMDP 54.4% (R19-R21).
statements.problem: The claim that recovery varies by dataset holds for this study, but the cited rows R1 (News, GAGD) and R14 (WMDP, GAKL) differ in method as well as dataset, so they don't isolate the domain effect.
